title: POC Weekly Sync - Dedicated Sizing & Autoscaling
summary: Weekly POC sync to review pilot performance, discuss Dedicated sizing, autoscaling policies, burst capacity, and next steps for running end-to-end benchmarks. Agreed to increase baseline capacity, test burst scenarios, and exchange a sizing spreadsheet and security docs.
topics: current traffic profile and peak patterns
action_items: Ben Liu: share recent 7-day qps and 95/99 latency csv by 2025-10-09
Daniel Cho: update Dedicated sizing spreadsheet with recommended slot counts by 2025-10-08
Ramesh Patel: run internal load test 2 with 10% synthetic burst and post results 2025-10-10
Sophie Martinez: share SOC2 and network diagram links by 2025-10-07
next_steps: Redwood to send updated Dedicated sizing spreadsheet and cost estimate
Customer to run two burst tests (10% and 50%) and share traces
Schedule deep-dive on autoscale policy tuning with SREs next week
Exchange security/architecture docs for Private deployment evaluation
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-06
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sophie (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood CSM); Aisha, Ben, Ramesh, Tara (Nexa)

[00:00] Sophie Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh it's our weekly sync on the Dedicated POC sizing. Quick check-in — any blockers before we dive in?
[00:12] Aisha Khan: No blockers, just want to make sure we cover burst planning, we saw a weird spike last week during data sync where latency went up.
[00:20] Daniel Cho: Yeah hi, Daniel here. We pulled the telemetry you sent, Ben, and ran a couple of sims; we'll go over that.
[00:30] Ben Liu: Cool thanks. Also, FYI, the spike was when our nightly report kicked off concurrent requests from several services.
[00:40] Sophie Martinez: Got it. Agenda: baseline sizing recap, autoscale policy options, burst planning, KV cache/batching impacts, and next steps.

[02:05] Daniel Cho: Quick baseline — based on the 95th percentile qps you shared last week we recommended starting with 4 dedicated slots on g5.2x for model X1-7b-quant. That gives you headroom for steady state plus small spikes.
[02:35] Ramesh Patel: Wait, the g5.2x mapping — can you remind us roughly how many concurrent streams per slot? We had different numbers in our internal doc.
[02:45] Daniel Cho: Sure, roughly 60 concurrent short-chat sessions per slot with our current batching defaults, but that depends a lot on sequence length and KV cache hit rate. For longer generations it's lower.

[04:10] Ben Liu: Our median seq len is about 120 tokens but the nightly report batches push that to 800 tokens. Could that explain the spike?
[04:22] Daniel Cho: Absolutely. Long sequences hold KV cache longer and increase GPU memory pressure — that reduces effective concurrency.
[04:35] Sophie Martinez: This is why burst planning matters. We can either provision burst capacity or tune autoscale to spike up quickly and then scale down. There's tradeoffs on cost vs. risk.

[06:00] Aisha Khan: For compliance reasons we prefer Dedicated over Hosted, but we need a predictable monthly cost. Bursting is fine as long as we have cost guardrails.
[06:15] Lena Ortiz: We can set burst caps and pre-warm slots; Redwood also supports a reserved baseline plus burst pool billing model. We'll include that in the sizing sheet.

[08:30] Daniel Cho: Talking autoscale: typical knobs are target utilization, scale step size, min/max slots, cool-down period. For low-latency apps we recommend aggressive scale-up (short cool-down) and conservative scale-down to avoid oscillation. Example: scale-up at 70% util with 30s evaluation window, cool-down 60-90s.
[09:05] Ramesh Patel: Does the evaluation window consider per-model queues or global? We run multiple routes to the same model version.
[09:15] Daniel Cho: Good question. Redwood can do per-route policies or a pooled policy; for your case if routes are independent we'd recommend per-route policies to avoid noisy neighbor effects.

[11:40] Ben Liu: What about prefix/KV caching impact? We saw a lot of repeated system prompts across sessions. Can caching reduce cost enough to change slot counts?
[11:52] Daniel Cho: Yes, prefix cache increases effective throughput. If your hit rate is 40-60% you could reduce slots by ~20-30% for the same latency SLO. But caching is most effective when sequences share prefixes or system prompts.

[13:30] Sophie Martinez: We ran a quick sensitivity matrix: with 50% KV hit and batching windows of 80ms, you need 3 slots instead of 4 for your 95th qps. We'll add those numbers to the sheet.

[15:05] Tara Singh: For the burst profile we want to test two cases: a 10% operational burst (expected) and a 50% stress burst (unlikely but good to understand). Can we simulate both?
[15:18] Daniel Cho: Yep, we recommend two tests: 10% sustained for 5 minutes and 50% for 2 minutes with ramp up. Measure queue lengths and 95/99 latency.

[17:00] Ramesh Patel: If we scale up quickly, how long does pre-warm take for a model with 70B parameters? Not relevant to X1-7b now, but for future planning.
[17:12] Daniel Cho: For huge models pre-warm can be 60-120s depending on storage and compilation. For the X1-7b quant it's more like 20-40s. We can use a warm pool for large models.

[19:30] Ben Liu: Cost — can you give a back-of-envelope for 4 slots baseline and 2-slot burst pool on g5?
[19:45] Sophie Martinez: We'll update the spreadsheet with regioned pricing; rough monthly estimate for the config you asked is in the doc we'll send, but approximate $Xk/month — specific number in the sheet.

[21:10] Aisha Khan: Security question — for Private deployment, how do keys and logs flow? We need a diagram for our security team.
[21:22] Lena Ortiz: We'll send the network diagram and KMS flow; Redwood supports customer-managed KMS and audit log exports to your SIEM. Sophie will share SOC 2 artifacts.

[23:00] Ben Liu: One more thing: our service occasionally sends 2000 concurrent short requests for a 30s period at midnight; will autoscale cope?
[23:12] Daniel Cho: If it's truly concurrent 2000 short sessions, you'd need many slots. But you can also queue with a frontend or use rate-limiting and prioritize critical routes. We should quantify that 2000 number into qps and average seq len to size appropriately.

[25:40] Sophie Martinez: Action item recap: Ben to share 7-day qps/latency CSV, Ramesh to run two burst tests, Daniel to update sizing sheet, Sophie to share security links.

[27:00] Ben Liu: I'll get the CSV by Friday, we have some dashboards that export it.
[27:10] Ramesh Patel: I'll run the synthetic bursts this week and post results.

[29:15] Daniel Cho: A couple of tuning tips: tune batching target latency to 50-80ms for chat-like workloads; that balances throughput and tail latency. Also consider adaptive batching — Redwood can enable dynamic batch sizes per route.

[31:00] Tara Singh: Do you have any concerns about model variants? We may want a smaller quant variant for low-latency mobile use.
[31:12] Daniel Cho: Yes, using a quantized smaller variant for low-latency is a common pattern — route mobile traffic to that model and desktop/heavy workflows to the full model. That also reduces burst capacity needs.

[33:40] Aisha Khan: Can you walk quickly through how cool-down and scale step size interplay? Example if we scale up by 2 slots each time vs scale up to target.
[33:55] Daniel Cho: If you scale up small steps you reduce overshoot but may be slower to reach capacity during sharp spikes. Scaling to target based on measured qps is faster but risks overprovisioning. For your case I'd recommend hybrid: scale-up to a fraction (e.g., +50% or +2 slots) with a short evaluation window, then if still above threshold scale to target.

[36:10] Ben Liu: For the 2000 short-request event, maybe we do a temporary policy that routes those requests to a heavier but cheaper async queue for non-critical work.
[36:22] Sophie Martinez: Right, queuing non-critical jobs is often cheaper than pure burst capacity. We'll document options.

[38:05] Ramesh Patel: Any gotchas with autoscale policies across regions? We have users in EU and US; can Redwood autoscale per-region?
[38:18] Daniel Cho: Yes, autoscale is per-cluster/region. We recommend independent policies by region because traffic patterns differ.

[40:30] Tara Singh: Benchmarks — would Redwood run a joint benchmark or do we run and share traces?
[40:42] Sophie Martinez: Usually customer runs the tests with our guidance because it's closer to production patterns; Redwood can run a validation benchmark afterward if you want. We'll provide a harness.

[42:00] Ben Liu: One last question — any guidance on min slots to keep cold-start probability low overnight?
[42:12] Daniel Cho: Keep a minimal baseline (e.g., 1 slot per region) and use a tiny warm pool for large models. Also use pre-warm triggers based on scheduled events.

[44:30] Sophie Martinez: Ok let's confirm commitments and timeline. Daniel will send updated sizing spreadsheet by tomorrow. Ben and Ramesh to run tests and post results by next Friday. Sophie to send SOC2, network diagram, and pricing sheet by Tuesday.

[46:00] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. Any other questions?

[47:00] Lena Ortiz: I'll open a shared thread and attach the sizing spreadsheet draft as soon as Daniel uploads it.

[48:05] Sophie Martinez: End of call — thanks all.

Note: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings and simplified speaker labels; refer to action items and attachments for authoritative details.
